original.rationale: Meta-analyses: US guidance reduces LA dose, lowers LAST incidence, may speed onset and reduce failures, fewer needle passes. Does not reliably reduce nerve injury vs nerve stim.

original.q: Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) inflation and deflation are timed to:
options: Inflate at end-diastole, deflate at peak systole
Inflate at the dicrotic notch (onset of diastole), deflate just before systole
Triggered by ECG R wave only without diastolic timing
original.rationale: IABP: inflates at the dicrotic notch (aortic valve closure → diastole) → augments coronary perfusion. Deflates just before systole → reduces afterload (↓LV work, ↑CO).

original.q: The most common reason for failed spinal anesthesia for cesarean delivery is:
options: Cephalad spread limited by pregnancy-related epidural compression
All can contribute, with inadequate dose / inadequate density most common
original.rationale: Cesarean spinal failure: dose too low, faulty technique (false-positive CSF return), too-rapid sit-up before block sets. Inadequate dose/density is most common overall.

original.q: Compared to adults, the MAC of sevoflurane in a 6-month-old is:
original.rationale: MAC peaks at age 1-6 months (sevoflurane ~3.2-3.3%) then decreases with age. Neonates have lower MAC than infants. Volatile uptake is faster in children (lower FRC, higher CO/alveolar ventilation).

original.q: During off-pump CABG, displacement of the heart for distal anastomoses commonly produces:
options: Severe hypotension and arrhythmia due to RV/LV obstruction or torsion
original.rationale: Off-pump (OPCAB) cardiac displacement → impaired filling, ventricular obstruction, MR, arrhythmia. Management: anticipate, fluid loading, vasopressor, Trendelenburg, TEE essential.

original.q: At 1 MAC of isoflurane, cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolic rate change:
original.rationale: Volatile anesthetics uncouple CBF and CMRO₂: cerebral vasodilation increases CBF while metabolic demand decreases — "luxury perfusion." Effect is dose-dependent.

original.q: Within the first 6 weeks postpartum, pregnancy-associated airway changes (edema, vascular engorgement):
options: Persist and may worsen with preeclampsia or fluid overload
original.rationale: Pregnancy airway changes take several weeks to resolve and may worsen with preeclampsia (capillary leak), fluid loading, prolonged pushing. Postpartum airway management still requires pregnancy-level precautions for at least 4-6 weeks.

original.q: Atropine pretreatment before pediatric RSI with succinylcholine is recommended primarily to prevent:
options: Bradycardia (especially with second dose or in infants <1 year)
original.rationale: Succinylcholine in children causes vagally mediated bradycardia, particularly in infants <1 year and with repeat dosing. Atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV (minimum 0.1 mg) pretreats.

original.q: Acute spinal cord injury at C5 causes which immediate hemodynamic finding?
options: Hypotension and bradycardia (neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic outflow)
original.rationale: Neurogenic shock (high SCI above T6): loss of sympathetic tone → hypotension + bradycardia (unopposed vagal). Distinguish from hypovolemic shock (tachycardia). Treat: fluids + NE, atropine for bradycardia.

original.q: TEE-derived ejection fraction estimation in the transgastric mid-papillary view assesses:
options: Left ventricular function and regional wall motion in all coronary distributions
original.rationale: TG-MID SAX: best single view for LV global function, EF, regional wall motion in all 3 coronary territories, and papillary muscle anatomy.

original.q: For an emergent stat cesarean delivery in a parturient without a working epidural and without IV access, the fastest induction of anesthesia is:
options: Inhalational induction with sevoflurane, then IV/intubation (rare scenario)
GA with rapid IV placement, preoxygenation, RSI with propofol/sux
original.rationale: Stat C/S no working epidural: GA with RSI (preoxygenate, propofol + sux, cricoid, intubate, low-dose volatile until cord clamped). Spinal possible if time allows (~5-7 min).

original.q: The earliest and most sensitive clinical sign of malignant hyperthermia (MH) is:
options: Unexplained rise in end-tidal CO₂ despite adequate ventilation
original.rationale: Rising ETCO₂ unresponsive to increased ventilation is the EARLIEST sensitive sign of MH — reflecting hypermetabolism. Hyperthermia is a LATE sign (can be 1-2°C/hr rise).

original.q: MH-triggering agents include:
original.rationale: MH triggers: all potent halogenated volatiles (sevo, des, iso) AND succinylcholine. SAFE: N₂O, propofol, etomidate, ketamine, opioids, benzodiazepines, all NDNMBs, all local anesthetics.

original.q: Initial dantrolene dose for active MH crisis is:
options: 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus, repeat every 5-10 min until resolved (up to 10+ mg/kg)
original.rationale: Dantrolene: 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus, repeat q5-10 min until signs resolve (commonly need 5-10+ mg/kg). After resolution: 1 mg/kg q6h × 24-48 h to prevent recurrence. MHAUS hotline: 1-800-644-9737.

original.q: The most common cause of anaphylaxis during anesthesia is:
original.rationale: Intraoperative anaphylaxis: NMBs ~60% (rocuronium and sux most common), latex 15-20% (declining), antibiotics, chlorhexidine. Cross-reactivity among NMBs via quaternary ammonium epitopes.

original.q: First-line treatment of severe intraoperative anaphylaxis is:
options: Epinephrine 10-100 mcg IV bolus (titrate to effect) + IV fluids
original.rationale: Anaphylaxis: epinephrine FIRST and FOREMOST. IV bolus 10-100 mcg, escalating to mg doses if needed; infusion if persistent. IV fluids (large volumes). Adjuncts: H1/H2 blockers, corticosteroids.

original.q: Serum tryptase confirming anaphylaxis should be drawn at:
options: Immediately after reaction and at 1-2 h (peak); compare with baseline (24+ h after) if possible
original.rationale: Mast cell tryptase peaks 30 min – 2 h after anaphylaxis, returns to baseline 12-24 h. Draw immediately and at 1-2 hours. Skin testing 4-6 weeks post-event to identify trigger.

original.q: Permissive hypotension in trauma resuscitation (without TBI) targets a systolic BP of approximately:
original.rationale: Permissive hypotension: target SBP 80-90 (MAP ~65) in penetrating trauma without TBI until surgical hemorrhage control — avoids exacerbating ongoing bleeding.

original.q: Succinylcholine should be avoided after major thermal injury starting:
options: After 24 hours and until at least 12 months post-injury (and possibly longer)
original.rationale: Sux is SAFE in the first 24 h. Upregulation of extrajunctional ACh receptors begins ~24-48 h, peaks 1-6 weeks, persists until full healing (~1 year). Risk: massive K⁺ release → cardiac arrest.

original.q: The Parkland formula for burn fluid resuscitation in the first 24 hours uses:
options: 4 mL/kg/% TBSA LR, half in first 8 h, remainder over next 16 h
original.rationale: Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA LR over 24 h (50% in first 8 h from time of burn). Titrate to urine output 0.5-1 mL/kg/h.

original.q: Elderly patients (>65) typically require what change in drug dosing?
options: Increased doses due to higher Vd
Decreased induction doses (e.g., propofol by 25-50%) and slower onset/offset
original.rationale: Aging: ↓lean mass, ↑fat, ↓CO, ↓renal/hepatic clearance, ↓protein binding. MAC decreases ~6%/decade after 40. Reduce propofol, opioids, midazolam by 25-50%. Postop delirium risk — avoid benzos.

original.q: Postoperative delirium in the elderly is reduced by all EXCEPT:
original.rationale: Delirium prevention: avoid Beers list drugs, dexmedetomidine for ICU sedation, multimodal analgesia, processed EEG monitoring (avoid burst suppression), early mobilization. Routine haloperidol prophylaxis has NOT consistently shown benefit.

original.q: Dosing of induction agents in morbid obesity generally uses:
options: Lean body weight or ideal body weight (e.g., propofol induction by LBW; maintenance by TBW)
original.rationale: Obese dosing: induction propofol — LBW; fentanyl — LBW; sux — TBW (↑ pseudocholinesterase); rocuronium — IBW; sugammadex — TBW; volatile MAC unchanged.

original.q: Patients with obstructive sleep apnea are at greatest perioperative risk for:
options: Difficult intubation, postoperative respiratory depression, and pulmonary complications
original.rationale: OSA risks: difficult mask ventilation and intubation, opioid-induced respiratory depression with collapse, atelectasis, pulmonary HTN/RV failure. STOP-BANG screening preop. Minimize opioids.

original.q: The WHO analgesic ladder for chronic pain places which agent at step 1?
original.rationale: WHO ladder: 1) Non-opioid ± adjuvant; 2) Add weak opioid; 3) Strong opioid. Modern multimodal approach targets multiple pathways for opioid sparing.

original.q: Gabapentinoids (gabapentin, pregabalin) act primarily by:
options: Binding the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in the CNS, reducing presynaptic glutamate release
original.rationale: Gabapentin/pregabalin bind α2δ-1 subunit of VGCCs → ↓Ca²⁺ influx → ↓neurotransmitter release. Useful for neuropathic pain and perioperative multimodal analgesia.

original.q: Standard adult IV morphine PCA settings include:
options: No basal, 1 mg demand, 6-10 min lockout, 4-hour limit
Variable, but basal infusion always required
original.rationale: Adult morphine IVPCA: demand 1 mg, lockout 6-10 min, 4-h limit ~20-30 mg. Basal infusions increase respiratory depression risk in opioid-naive patients — avoid.

original.q: Multimodal analgesia after major abdominal surgery typically includes:
options: Acetaminophen + NSAID/COX-2 + opioid + regional (epidural or TAP) + adjuvants (ketamine, gabapentinoid, dexmedetomidine) as appropriate
original.rationale: ERAS multimodal analgesia: scheduled APAP + NSAID (ketorolac), epidural or TAP block, low-dose ketamine, gabapentinoid (pre-induction), dexamethasone, dexmedetomidine, magnesium, opioid-sparing.

original.q: The FLACC scale for pediatric pain assessment evaluates:
original.rationale: FLACC pain scale (children 2 months–7 years): Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability — each 0-2, total 0-10.

original.q: After episode of intraoperative awareness, the most important intervention is:
options: Reassure the patient that this never happens again
Acknowledge, apologize, listen, screen for PTSD symptoms, refer for mental health support, root-cause analysis
Charge a fee for additional anesthesia
original.rationale: Awareness with recall is psychologically traumatic — up to 50% develop PTSD. Approach: acknowledge, validate, apologize, structured interview, mental health referral, identify cause, document.

original.q: TURP syndrome from hypotonic irrigation absorption presents with:
options: Dilutional hyponatremia, fluid overload, cerebral edema, hemolysis (depending on irrigant)
original.rationale: TURP syndrome: absorption of hypotonic irrigation (glycine 1.5%, sorbitol, mannitol) through prostatic venous sinuses → dilutional hyponatremia, fluid overload, visual disturbances, seizures, cerebral edema.

original.q: Patients at highest risk for latex allergy include all EXCEPT:
options: Patients with spina bifida or urogenital anomalies (repeated catheterization)
Patients with multiple surgeries from infancy
original.rationale: Latex allergy risk: healthcare workers, spina bifida, repeated GU/GI surgery from infancy, atopy, cross-reactive foods (avocado, banana, kiwi, chestnut — "latex-fruit syndrome"). Smoking/COPD is NOT a risk factor.

original.q: Stress-induced hyperglycemia perioperatively should target a blood glucose of approximately:
original.rationale: NICE-SUGAR (2009): intensive glucose control (81-108) increased mortality vs conventional (<180). Current SCCM/ADA recommendation: perioperative glucose 140-180 mg/dL.

original.q: Thyroid storm during surgery is treated with all EXCEPT:
options: Iodine (Lugol's solution) at least 1 h after PTU/methimazole
original.rationale: Thyroid storm: beta-blockade, PTU/methimazole, iodine (after antithyroids), corticosteroids, cooling (acetaminophen — NOT aspirin, which displaces T4 from binding proteins and worsens). Treat trigger.

original.q: Preoperative preparation of pheochromocytoma requires:
options: Alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 10-14 days before adding beta-blocker as needed
original.rationale: Pheo: ALPHA-blockade FIRST (phenoxybenzamine 10-40 mg BID or doxazosin) for 10-14 days, then β-blockade ONLY after alpha (unopposed α with β-block first → hypertensive crisis).

original.q: Intraoperative hypertensive crisis during pheochromocytoma manipulation is best treated with:
original.rationale: Pheo crisis: short-acting agents — nitroprusside, nicardipine (preferred at many centers), phentolamine (classic α-blocker). After tumor ligation — hypotension common → fluids, NE, vasopressin.

original.q: Myasthenia gravis patients show abnormal sensitivity to which NMB class?
options: Resistance to succinylcholine, sensitivity to nondepolarizers
Sensitivity to nondepolarizers; variable response to succinylcholine (often resistance)
original.rationale: MG (anti-AChR antibodies, fewer functional receptors): VERY SENSITIVE to nondepolarizers (use ~10-50% dose, TOF monitoring); RESISTANT to succinylcholine (need higher dose).

original.q: Perioperative management of sickle cell disease aims to prevent sickling by avoiding:
options: Hypoxia, hypothermia, acidosis, dehydration, stasis, infection
original.rationale: Sickling triggers: hypoxia, hypothermia, hypovolemia/dehydration, acidosis, hypotension, stasis, infection. Prevent: aggressive O₂, warming, balanced fluids, normothermia, ± exchange transfusion (HbS <30%).

original.q: In chronic kidney disease (CKD), which drug should be AVOIDED for prolonged paralysis risk?
original.rationale: Vecuronium is primarily hepatic/biliary and renal-cleared → dramatically prolonged in CKD. Pancuronium similarly. Prefer cisatracurium (Hofmann elimination — organ-independent).

original.q: Pseudocholinesterase is synthesized by the liver. In severe liver failure, succinylcholine effect is:
options: Prolonged due to reduced pseudocholinesterase levels (clinically modest unless severe)
original.rationale: Pseudocholinesterase is hepatic-synthesized. Decreased in severe liver disease → succinylcholine duration prolonged but usually <30 min unless atypical enzyme or extreme deficiency.

original.q: Coagulopathy in advanced liver disease results from:
options: Decreased synthesis of all coagulation factors EXCEPT VIII and vWF; also decreased anticoagulants (protein C/S, AT) — balanced "rebalanced" coagulation
original.rationale: Liver synthesizes most coag factors (except VIII, vWF). Also synthesizes anticoagulants (protein C/S, AT III). "Rebalanced hemostasis" — INR prolonged but thrombosis risk preserved. TEG/ROTEM more useful than INR.

original.q: The earliest perioperative benefit of smoking cessation occurs within:
options: 24 hours: COHb falls, oxygen delivery improves
8+ weeks: marked decrease in pulm complications
Smoking cessation has no perioperative benefit
original.rationale: "No benefit in stopping right before" is a myth — even 24-h cessation improves oxygen delivery (COHb halves). Optimal cessation is ≥8 weeks before surgery for major pulmonary benefits.

original.q: Diabetic gastroparesis affects anesthetic management primarily by:
options: Increasing risk of perioperative aspiration — full-stomach precautions
original.rationale: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy: gastroparesis → full stomach risk → RSI even after fasting. Other DM concerns: difficult airway (stiff joint syndrome), CAD, nephropathy, neuropathy.

original.q: All of the following are contraindicated in pheochromocytoma EXCEPT:
original.rationale: AVOID in pheo: indirect sympathomimetics (ephedrine, dopamine), glucagon (stimulates catecholamine release), metoclopramide and droperidol (dopamine antagonism → catecholamine release). Phenylephrine acceptable after alpha blockade.

original.q: Anti-platelet management before elective non-cardiac surgery in a patient with recent (3-month) drug-eluting stent should:
options: Stop ASA and P2Y12 5 days before
Delay surgery if possible until DAPT complete (≥6-12 months); continue ASA throughout
Bridge with heparin and stop all antiplatelets
Stop just P2Y12 the morning of surgery
original.rationale: Recent DES (within 6 months): delay elective surgery until DAPT complete. For urgent surgery: continue ASA, hold P2Y12 (clopidogrel 5-7 d). Heparin bridging is NOT helpful (platelet-mediated).

original.q: A patient's DNR order in the perioperative period:
options: Must be addressed (required reconsideration) with the patient/surrogate to determine which interventions are wanted intraoperatively
original.rationale: ASA Ethical Guidelines: DNR orders should NOT be automatically suspended in the OR — require reconsideration with the patient/surrogate to determine scope of acceptable interventions.

original.q: Application of a magnet to a permanent pacemaker generally causes:
options: Asynchronous (DOO or VOO) pacing at a manufacturer-specific rate
original.rationale: Magnet over pacemaker → asynchronous mode (DOO or VOO) at programmed magnet rate (usually 85-100 bpm). Magnet over ICD → suspends arrhythmia detection/therapy (does NOT change pacing mode).

original.q: Mild perioperative hypothermia (~1°C below normal) is associated with all EXCEPT:
original.rationale: Inadvertent perioperative hypothermia: wound infection, coagulopathy, prolonged drug effects, shivering (↑O₂ consumption 400%). INCREASES (not decreases) postop pain.

original.q: After confirmed awareness with recall, the patient should be:
options: Re-anesthetized with same technique to demonstrate it works
Counseled about the event, screened for PTSD, and root-cause analysis performed
original.rationale: Post-awareness approach: acknowledge, validate, apologize, identify and explain cause, mental health referral (PTSD rates up to 50%), risk management consult, document, plan future anesthetics.

original.q: Chronic alcohol use affects MAC by:
original.rationale: Chronic ethanol use: upregulates GABA receptors, induces CYP2E1 → cross-tolerance to volatiles, benzodiazepines, opioids. Acute intoxication: REDUCED dose required (synergistic with anesthetics).

original.q: An opioid-tolerant patient on 200 MME/day requires which postoperative pain strategy?
options: Maintain baseline opioid (often via PCA basal or scheduled), add multimodal non-opioids, regional anesthesia, ketamine, dexmedetomidine; expect higher total opioid requirement
original.rationale: Opioid-tolerant patient: maintain baseline opioids (avoid withdrawal), aggressive multimodal — regional, ketamine, dexmedetomidine, gabapentinoids, NSAIDs/APAP. Expect 30-100% above baseline for acute pain.

original.q: A patient on buprenorphine 16 mg/day for opioid use disorder requires surgery. Current best practice is:
options: Continue buprenorphine, manage pain with multimodal analgesia + full-agonist opioid (often higher doses needed)
original.rationale: Modern guidance: CONTINUE buprenorphine perioperatively. Stopping risks relapse. Buprenorphine has high mu affinity but partial activity — full agonist opioids still work at higher doses. Combine with regional, ketamine, multimodal.

original.q: Open-globe injury anesthesia traditionally avoids succinylcholine because of fear of:
options: Increased intraocular pressure causing extrusion of contents (limited modern evidence)
original.rationale: Sux briefly increases IOP (~6-8 mmHg). Modern view: sux generally acceptable with full RSI. Rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg is acceptable alternative.

original.q: Hyperalgesia after high-dose remifentanil intraoperatively is mediated by:
options: NMDA receptor activation and other proalgesic mechanisms
original.rationale: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH), especially with remifentanil, involves NMDA receptor activation and descending facilitation. Mitigation: ketamine adjunct, magnesium, gradual remi taper, multimodal.

original.q: In severe accidental hypothermia (core temp <30°C) with cardiac arrest, ACLS modifications include:
options: Withhold drugs until temperature >30°C (medication metabolism unpredictable)
Continue ACLS exactly as in normothermia
original.rationale: Severe hypothermia (<30°C): drugs accumulate (unpredictable metabolism); withhold/space ACLS medications until core >30°C. Defibrillation may be ineffective until rewarmed. "Not dead until warm and dead."

original.q: Emergency cricothyroidotomy in "cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate" situation is performed at:
options: Cricothyroid membrane between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages
original.rationale: Cricothyroidotomy: cricothyroid membrane (between thyroid cartilage above, cricoid cartilage below) — palpable as a soft "V" below the laryngeal prominence. Preferred technique: scalpel-finger-bougie.

original.q: After uneventful intubation, EtCO₂ reads 0 mmHg. The most concerning possibility is:
options: Both A: this dual question essentially asks identify and treat: confirm tube placement and pulse
original.rationale: ZERO EtCO₂ after intubation: esophageal intubation, cardiac arrest, complete airway disconnect, capnograph failure. CONFIRM immediately. "No CO₂ = no chance."

original.q: A patient on MAOI inhibitors requires emergency surgery. Which agent should be avoided?
options: Meperidine and ephedrine (serotonin syndrome / hypertensive crisis)
original.rationale: MAOIs: AVOID meperidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan (serotonin syndrome — fatal); avoid indirect sympathomimetics ephedrine, dopamine (excessive NE release → hypertensive crisis). SAFE: morphine, fentanyl (carefully), direct vasopressors.

original.q: After an episode of intraoperative dental injury, the standard initial response includes:
options: Document, locate the tooth/fragment (chest X-ray to rule out aspiration), refer to dentistry, disclose to patient
original.rationale: Dental injuries: most common anesthesia closed-claim malpractice event. After injury: locate fragment (CXR if missing — aspiration could be catastrophic), preserve, refer to dentist, document, disclose to patient.

original.q: For general anesthesia for cesarean delivery, the typical induction agent dose adjustment is:
options: Increased due to volume of distribution
Lower doses considered (less for placental transfer); rapid sequence with cricoid; minimize volatile until cord clamped
original.rationale: Cesarean GA: RSI — propofol 2 mg/kg + sux 1.5 mg/kg + cricoid. Low-dose volatile (0.5 MAC) until cord clamped to minimize fetal exposure. After clamping: increase MAC + opioids.

original.q: The Bezold-Jarisch reflex in spinal anesthesia produces:
options: Bradycardia and hypotension triggered by venous return reduction sensing
original.rationale: Bezold-Jarisch reflex: empty ventricle/under-filled LV stimulates vagal afferents → reflex bradycardia, hypotension, vasodilation. Seen in high spinal, hypovolemia, vasovagal. Treatment: IV fluids, ephedrine, atropine.

original.q: The single most important spirometric predictor of post-pneumonectomy pulmonary function is:
options: Predicted postoperative FEV1 (ppoFEV1) calculated using lung segments
original.rationale: ppoFEV1 = preop FEV1 × (1 – fraction of lung removed). ppoFEV1 >40% = generally safe; <30% = high risk. Cardiopulmonary exercise test (VO₂max) if borderline.

original.q: Severe intraoperative bronchospasm in an asthmatic is best managed initially by:
options: Deepening anesthesia (volatile bronchodilation), 100% O₂, inhaled beta-2 agonist via ETT (8-10 puffs)
original.rationale: Intraoperative bronchospasm: deepen anesthesia (sevo > iso > des), 100% O₂, albuterol 8-10 puffs through ETT, epinephrine (10-100 mcg IV) if severe, IV steroids (delayed effect). Avoid morphine, atracurium (histamine).

original.q: Mechanical ventilation in a COPD patient with hyperinflation and auto-PEEP should:
options: Use long inspiratory times with high TV
Use prolonged expiratory time (low I:E ratio, e.g., 1:3-1:5), allow permissive hypercapnia, low TV (6 mL/kg IBW)
original.rationale: COPD ventilation: avoid air-trapping/auto-PEEP. Strategy: low rate (8-12), long expiratory time (I:E 1:3-1:5), low TV 6-8 mL/kg IBW, permissive hypercapnia. Disconnect briefly if severe gas-trapping → cardiovascular collapse.

original.q: In a patient with severe pulmonary hypertension, anesthetic goals include:
options: Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis (all worsen PVR), avoid N₂O, maintain RV preload, maintain coronary perfusion, use inhaled NO/prostacyclin if needed
original.rationale: Pulmonary HTN: avoid PVR-raising factors (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, N₂O). Maintain RV function: preload optimization (cautious), maintain systemic BP for RV coronary supply. Inhaled NO 20-40 ppm.

original.q: A patient with EF 25% (heart failure with reduced EF) tolerates which induction agent best?
original.rationale: Low EF: etomidate ideal — preserves hemodynamics. Ketamine useful if not catecholamine-depleted. Propofol: profound vasodilation/cardiac depression — slow titration or avoid. Avoid pancuronium (tachycardia).

original.q: In Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome with pre-excited atrial fibrillation, which drug is contraindicated?
options: Adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin (all block AV node → preferential conduction down accessory pathway → 1:1 ventricular response → VF)
original.rationale: WPW + pre-excited AFib: AV nodal blockers → antegrade conduction down accessory pathway → rapid VR (>250 bpm) → degenerates to VF. Use procainamide, ibutilide, or DC cardioversion.

original.q: Acute kidney injury (AKI) by KDIGO criteria includes any of:
options: Cr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48h, or 1.5× baseline in 7 days, or UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6+ hours
original.rationale: KDIGO AKI: Cr ≥0.3 mg/dL rise in 48 h OR ≥1.5× baseline in 7 d OR UO <0.5 mL/kg/h × 6 h. Staged 1-3 by severity.

original.q: Dialysis-dependent CKD patients should NOT receive which volume expander?
options: Normal saline (large volumes cause hyperchloremic acidosis and hyperkalemia)
Lactated Ringer's (K+ 4 mEq/L) — concern is overstated; usually safe
Both A and the K+ in LR matter; minimize chloride
original.rationale: ESRD volume management: avoid chloride-rich NS in large volumes (→ hyperchloremic acidosis → ↑K). LR's K (4 mEq/L) usually safe in small-moderate volumes. Minimize chloride load overall.

original.q: Child-Pugh class C cirrhosis is associated with perioperative mortality for major abdominal surgery of approximately:
original.rationale: Child-Pugh: A (5-6 pts, mortality ~10%), B (7-9, ~30%), C (10-15, 75%+). MELD score: predicts 90-day mortality. >15 = contraindication for elective non-transplant surgery.

original.q: Stress-dose steroid coverage is INDICATED in which patient?
options: Patient on prednisone 5 mg/day for <1 month
Patient on prednisone 20 mg/day for >3 weeks
Patient who stopped prednisone 6 months ago
original.rationale: HPA suppression risk: prednisone ≥5 mg/d for ≥3 weeks (or equivalent). Coverage for major surgery: 100 mg hydrocortisone at induction + 50-100 mg q8h × 24-48h.

original.q: Which opioid is generally PREFERRED in patients with severe renal impairment?
options: Fentanyl or hydromorphone (fewer renally cleared active metabolites)
original.rationale: ESRD opioids: AVOID morphine (M6G accumulates), meperidine (normeperidine — seizures), codeine (unpredictable). PREFER fentanyl, hydromorphone, methadone, buprenorphine.

original.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) intraoperatively presents with:
options: Hyperglycemia, anion-gap metabolic acidosis, ketonuria, dehydration
original.rationale: DKA: glucose >250, AGMA (pH <7.3, HCO₃ <18), ketonuria/ketonemia. Treatment: IV insulin infusion (after volume + K⁺ check), aggressive fluid resuscitation, replace K⁺.

original.q: Hereditary spherocytosis patients undergoing splenectomy require:
options: Pre- and postoperative vaccination against encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib)
original.rationale: Splenectomy preparation: vaccinate ≥2 weeks before elective surgery against Strep pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae type b. Risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI).

original.q: Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) for perioperative MACE includes all EXCEPT:
original.rationale: RCRI (Lee Index) — 6 factors: 1) high-risk surgery, 2) IHD, 3) CHF, 4) CVD (TIA/stroke), 5) insulin-treated DM, 6) Cr >2 mg/dL. ≥2 factors → elevated risk. Mild HTN is NOT in RCRI.

original.q: Functional capacity <4 METs (e.g., cannot climb a flight of stairs) is associated with:
options: Higher perioperative cardiac risk and potential indication for further evaluation
original.rationale: Functional capacity in METs: 1=eating, 4=climbing stairs, 10=strenuous sports. <4 METs = poor functional capacity = increased cardiac risk. ACC/AHA algorithm: if MET <4 + elevated risk → consider noninvasive testing.

original.q: Parkinson disease patients should:
options: Have all medications stopped 24 h preop
Continue antiparkinsonian medications including dose on morning of surgery; avoid metoclopramide, droperidol, phenothiazines (worsen symptoms)
original.rationale: Parkinson: continue carbidopa-levodopa (short half-life — withdrawal → severe rigidity, dysphagia, respiratory failure). Avoid D2 antagonists (metoclopramide, droperidol, phenothiazines). Safe antiemetics: ondansetron, dexamethasone.

original.q: Multiple sclerosis patients undergoing surgery should:
options: Avoid all neuraxial anesthesia (controversial — see explanation)
Be informed about possible exacerbation; maintain normothermia (hyperthermia exacerbates demyelination)
original.rationale: MS: perioperative exacerbation risk (heat, stress, infection). HYPERTHERMIA worsens conduction block — keep normothermic (Uhthoff phenomenon). Neuraxial: not absolutely contraindicated; document discussion.

original.q: Carcinoid crisis triggered by tumor manipulation is best managed by:
options: Octreotide bolus (50-100 mcg) ± infusion, IV fluids, vasopressors as needed (avoid catecholamines that may worsen flushing)
original.rationale: Carcinoid crisis: octreotide bolus, fluids, careful vasopressors (catecholamines may trigger more mediator release → phenylephrine preferred). Pre-op octreotide infusion essential. Avoid histamine releasers (morphine, sux).

original.q: A patient with Mobitz type II second-degree AV block typically requires:
options: Permanent pacemaker before elective surgery, or temporary perioperatively
original.rationale: Mobitz II (infranodal block): high risk of progression to complete heart block, especially under anesthesia. Permanent pacemaker before elective surgery (or temporary pacing pads ready).

original.q: Severe hypothyroidism (myxedema coma) anesthetic implications include:
options: Decreased MAC, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hyponatremia, slow drug metabolism, sensitive to anesthetics
original.rationale: Severe hypothyroidism: ↓MAC, hypothermia, ↓CO, bradycardia, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, slow metabolism, exquisite sensitivity to anesthetics, delayed gastric emptying. Defer elective surgery.

original.q: One-lung ventilation (OLV) physiology relies on:
options: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) redirecting blood from non-ventilated to ventilated lung
PEEP applied only to non-ventilated lung
original.rationale: HPV: alveolar hypoxia → local pulmonary vasoconstriction → blood redirected to better-ventilated alveoli → IMPROVES V/Q. HPV inhibited by volatile anesthetics (>1 MAC). Optimize OLV: TV 4-6 mL/kg IBW, CPAP to non-ventilated.

original.q: Aortic cross-clamping at the supraceliac level causes which immediate hemodynamic change?
options: Severe decrease in afterload and hypotension
Marked increase in SVR/afterload, increase in proximal MAP, decrease in distal organ perfusion (kidneys, viscera, spinal cord)
original.rationale: Aortic XC → ↑↑SVR (proximal HTN), ↑LV wall stress, ↓distal perfusion (renal, gut, cord), metabolic acidosis. At clamp release: distributive vasodilation → hypotension.

original.q: DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) management focuses primarily on:
options: Treating the underlying cause (sepsis, trauma, obstetric, malignancy) + supportive blood products as bleeding/clinical condition dictate
original.rationale: DIC: address underlying trigger (sepsis, AFE, abruption, trauma, malignancy). Supportive: cryo (fibrinogen <100-150), FFP, platelets (<50 with bleeding). Heparin controversial — primarily for chronic compensated thrombotic DIC.

original.q: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) ventilation strategy includes:
options: TV 12 mL/kg actual body weight, PEEP 0
TV 6 mL/kg IBW, plateau pressure ≤30, optimized PEEP, FiO₂ lowest tolerable, permissive hypercapnia, prone positioning for severe
original.rationale: ARDSnet: TV 6 mL/kg IBW, Pplat ≤30, PEEP per FiO₂ ladder, permissive hypercapnia (pH ≥7.2), driving pressure goal <14. Prone positioning for moderate-severe ARDS (P/F <150) → 16+ h/day.

original.q: Anesthetic agents safe in severe hepatic dysfunction include all EXCEPT:
options: Sevoflurane and isoflurane at usual MAC
original.rationale: Halothane hepatitis (rare, immune-mediated) historically led to its decline. Modern volatiles (iso, des, sevo) less hepatotoxic. Cisatracurium (Hofmann elimination) and remifentanil (esterase) are ideal.

original.q: SGLT-2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) should be held preoperatively because of risk of:
original.rationale: SGLT-2 inhibitors: perioperative stress + fasting + ketogenic milieu → euDKA (normal/mildly elevated glucose but AGMA and ketosis). FDA: hold 3-4 days preop.

original.q: Aortic regurgitation anesthetic goals favor:
options: Fast HR (shortens diastole, reduces regurgitant volume), reduced afterload, maintained preload
original.rationale: Severe AR goals: "full, fast, forward." Higher HR (80-100) reduces diastolic time → less regurgitation. Avoid bradycardia. Maintain preload, reduce afterload (vasodilators improve forward flow).

original.q: Mitral regurgitation anesthetic goals favor:
options: Normal-to-high HR, low SVR (afterload reduction promotes forward flow), euvolemia, avoid pulmonary HTN
original.rationale: MR: "full, fast, vasodilated." Reduce afterload (less regurgitation, more forward flow). Maintain HR 80-100. Avoid factors raising PVR and sudden ↑SVR.

original.q: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is best managed by:
options: Stopping all heparin, starting non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux), avoiding warfarin until platelets recover
original.rationale: HIT: STOP all heparin (including flushes, heparin-coated catheters). Bridge with argatroban or bivalirudin. Don't start warfarin until platelets >150 (warfarin-induced limb gangrene). LMWH cross-reacts — avoid.

original.q: von Willebrand disease type 1 (most common type) is best treated perioperatively with:
options: DDAVP (desmopressin) 0.3 mcg/kg IV — releases vWF from endothelium
original.rationale: vWD type 1 (quantitative deficiency): DDAVP 0.3 mcg/kg IV increases vWF/F-VIII 3-5x within 30 min. Test response preop. Tachyphylaxis after 2-3 doses. Type 2B contraindicated for DDAVP. Type 3 requires vWF concentrate.

original.q: Pacemaker code letter 1 designates:
original.rationale: NBG pacing code: I — Chamber Paced (A, V, D = dual, O = none); II — Chamber Sensed; III — Response (I = inhibited, T = triggered, D = dual); IV — Rate modulation (R); V — Multisite.

original.q: Coronary anatomy: the LAD (left anterior descending) artery supplies:
options: Anterior wall, anteroseptal LV, anterolateral papillary muscle, most of interventricular septum
original.rationale: LAD: anterior LV, anteroseptal, apex, anterior 2/3 of septum, anterolateral papillary. LCX: lateral wall. RCA: inferior LV, RV, AV node (90%), SA node (60%), posterior 1/3 of septum (right-dominant).

original.q: Status epilepticus during anesthesia is best treated initially with:
options: Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (or midazolam 0.2 mg/kg if no IV) — first line
original.rationale: Status epilepticus: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV first-line; if no IV — midazolam 10 mg IM. Second-line: fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, valproate. Refractory: propofol or pentobarbital infusion with EEG.

original.q: The principal causes of perioperative acute kidney injury include all EXCEPT:
original.rationale: Perioperative AKI causes: prerenal (hypotension, hypovolemia, low CO), intrarenal (nephrotoxins, sepsis-ATN, rhabdo), postrenal. Mild HTN does NOT cause AKI.

original.q: A trauma patient with massive transfusion develops hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. This "lethal triad":
options: Is mutually reinforcing — each worsens the others and increases mortality dramatically
original.rationale: Trauma "lethal triad": hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy mutually reinforce → mortality cascade. Prevention: warm patient/fluids, buffer pH if extreme, balanced 1:1:1 resuscitation, TXA, damage-control surgery.

original.q: Cell salvage (intraoperative autologous transfusion) is contraindicated in which scenario?
options: Surgery in infected or malignant fields (relative — controversial, used with leukocyte-depletion filters in many centers)
original.rationale: Cell salvage contraindications: traditionally infected field (sepsis risk) and malignancy (theoretical tumor seeding), although modern leukocyte-depletion filters allow use in many cancer cases.

original.q: Pituitary surgery anesthetic considerations include:
options: Smooth induction, avoid coughing/bucking, plan for transsphenoidal positioning with eye protection, anticipate diabetes insipidus postop, hormonal coverage (stress steroids if pan-hypopituitarism)
original.rationale: Pituitary surgery: smooth induction, throat pack (count carefully), VAE risk (variable), postop diabetes insipidus (polyuria → DDAVP), hormone replacement, stress steroids if cortisol deficient.

original.q: VAE (venous air embolism) treatment includes all EXCEPT:
options: Flood surgical field with saline; pack venous source
Left lateral decubitus, Trendelenburg (to keep air in right atrium)
Aspirate from CVP / multi-orifice catheter in RA
original.rationale: VAE treatment: stop entrainment (flood field), 100% O₂, STOP N₂O (expands bubbles 34×), Durant position (left lateral + Trendelenburg), aspirate from CVC. Hyperventilation NOT routine.

original.q: Cryoprecipitate is the appropriate product for:
options: Replacement of fibrinogen (<150 mg/dL with bleeding), Factor VIII, vWF, Factor XIII, fibronectin
original.rationale: Cryoprecipitate: cold-precipitated from FFP. Rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII, fibronectin. Dose: 1 unit/10 kg raises fibrinogen ~50 mg/dL.

original.q: Kidney transplant anesthesia (recipient) typically uses:
options: GA with avoidance of nephrotoxins, careful fluid management (often liberal hydration, mannitol for graft perfusion, mannitol/furosemide for diuresis at reperfusion), avoidance of pancuronium (renal clearance)
original.rationale: Kidney transplant: GA most common. Liberal fluids (CVP 10-15) for graft perfusion. Mannitol 0.5 g/kg + furosemide 0.5 mg/kg at vascular clamp release. Cisatracurium preferred. Watch for reperfusion hyperkalemia.

original.q: TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) procedure anesthesia considerations include:
options: Awareness of bleeding from varices, hepatic encephalopathy worsening, low cardiac reserve (cirrhotic cardiomyopathy), volume shifts at shunt creation
original.rationale: TIPS: usually MAC/sedation, sometimes GA. Cirrhosis concerns — coagulopathy, encephalopathy (avoid benzos), hyperdynamic state, hepatopulmonary syndrome. Shunt creation: portal pressure drops → hemodynamic shifts.

original.q: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are reduced by:
options: Lung-protective ventilation, regional/multimodal analgesia for thoracic/abdominal incisions, early ambulation, incentive spirometry, smoking cessation, treating wheezing preop
original.rationale: PPC prevention: lung-protective ventilation (TV 6-8/PEEP 5/Pplat<16), opioid-sparing analgesia (regional, epidural), early ambulation, incentive spirometry, smoking cessation, CPAP for OSA.

original.q: EEG burst suppression during anesthesia is associated with:
options: Increased postoperative delirium and possibly mortality in elderly — minimize unnecessary burst suppression
original.rationale: Burst suppression: associated with postop delirium (elderly especially) and possibly mortality. Required only for specific neurosurgical cases (cerebral protection) and refractory status epilepticus. Use processed EEG to avoid.

original.q: Tricuspid regurgitation in an adult with pulmonary HTN is best managed by:
options: Maintain RV function: avoid factors raising PVR, support coronary perfusion of RV (systemic BP), gentle inotropic support (milrinone, dobutamine), iNO
original.rationale: TR with PH: "protect the RV." Avoid PVR triggers. Maintain systemic BP for RV coronary supply. Inotropic support if RV failing — milrinone (PDE3, reduces PVR), dobutamine, iNO for selective pulmonary vasodilation.

original.q: Bronchopleural fistula anesthesia: best strategy for one-lung ventilation is:
options: Awake intubation with bronchial blocker or double-lumen tube to isolate fistula side; avoid positive-pressure ventilation across fistula
original.rationale: BPF: positive pressure → air leak through fistula → tension pneumothorax. Awake fiberoptic intubation if possible. DLT or bronchial blocker isolates fistula side. Avoid high airway pressures.

original.q: Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) prevention strategies include:
options: Aggressive hydration (IV saline or isotonic bicarbonate around contrast administration); avoid nephrotoxins; minimize contrast volume; use iso-osmolar contrast
original.rationale: CIN prevention: hydration is most effective. N-acetylcysteine — mixed evidence; many guidelines no longer recommend it. Avoid concurrent nephrotoxins, minimize contrast volume, low-osmolar or iso-osmolar contrast.

original.q: Acromegaly anesthetic implications include all EXCEPT:
options: Difficult airway (large tongue, mandible, soft tissues, narrowed glottis)
original.rationale: Acromegaly: airway (macroglossia, prognathism, glottic stenosis), cardiomyopathy (LVH, diastolic dysfunction), HTN, OSA, DM, peripheral neuropathy. MAC is UNCHANGED — not decreased.

original.q: Tumor lysis syndrome in oncology patients undergoing surgery presents with:
options: Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia, hypocalcemia, possible AKI
original.rationale: TLS: rapid cell lysis → release of intracellular contents. Hyper-K, hyper-PO₄ (→ binds Ca → hypoCa), hyper-uricemia → AKI. Prevention: aggressive hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase.

original.q: Severe pulmonary hypertension in a patient for non-cardiac surgery — anesthetic considerations include:
options: Routine spinal anesthesia regardless of severity

Avoid factors increasing PVR (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, light anesthesia, N₂O), support RV function, careful fluid balance, available pulmonary vasodilators (NO, prostacyclin), TEE monitoring for major surgery
Aggressive vasodilation with nitroprusside as first-line
Liberal fluid bolus loading throughout the case
TIVA only — volatile anesthetics are absolutely contraindicated
original.rationale: Severe pulmonary HTN: high perioperative mortality (up to 18%). Continue chronic pulm vasodilators. Avoid PVR triggers. TEE, careful fluid balance. Inhaled NO (20-40 ppm) or inhaled prostacyclin for refractory crisis.

original.q: The most common cause of perioperative acute kidney injury is:
options: Pre-renal hypoperfusion from hypovolemia, hypotension, and low cardiac output
original.rationale: Perioperative AKI is largely pre-renal — hypovolemia, hypotension (MAP <65 for sustained periods), low CO. Prevent: MAP >65 (higher in CKD/HTN), maintain euvolemia (balanced crystalloid > NS), avoid nephrotoxins.

original.q: Postoperative pulmonary complications are most strongly reduced by which intraoperative strategy?
options: Lung-protective ventilation (TV 6-8 mL/kg IBW, PEEP, low driving pressure) plus minimize aspiration, multimodal analgesia, early extubation when appropriate
High tidal volume to prevent atelectasis
original.rationale: PPC prevention bundle: lung-protective ventilation, aspiration prevention, opioid-sparing analgesia (regional > opioid), full NMB reversal (TOF ratio >0.9), incentive spirometry/early ambulation, smoking cessation.

original.q: What is the standard pipeline working pressure for oxygen, nitrous oxide, and medical air delivered to the anesthesia machine?
original.rationale: Hospital pipeline systems supply all medical gases (O2, N2O, medical air) at approximately 50–55 psi. This standardized working pressure allows the anesthesia machine to accept pipeline gas without additional high-pressure reduction.

original.q: A full E-cylinder of oxygen reads approximately 2,200 psi. After using half its contents, what pressure would you expect?
options: 745 psi (pressure stays constant until nearly empty)
original.rationale: Oxygen is stored as a compressed gas — its pressure is directly proportional to the remaining volume. A half-full O2 E-cylinder contains ~330 L and reads approximately 1,100 psi. This is in contrast to nitrous oxide, which is stored as a liquid and maintains constant pressure until all liquid evaporates.

original.q: You need to estimate how much nitrous oxide remains in an E-cylinder. The pressure gauge reads 500 psi. What is the most accurate way to determine remaining volume?
options: Assume 50% remains since pressure is below 745 psi
Calculate using the formula: Volume = Pressure × 0.3 ÷ Flow rate
Weigh the cylinder; pressure alone is unreliable for N2O
Trust the gauge — 500 psi indicates approximately 1/3 full
original.rationale: N2O is stored as a liquid in equilibrium with its vapor. The pressure gauge reads vapor pressure (~745 psi) regardless of how much liquid remains. Once all liquid evaporates, pressure drops rapidly. The only accurate method to determine remaining N2O volume is to weigh the cylinder.

original.q: Which safety system prevents attaching the wrong gas cylinder to the wrong yoke on the anesthesia machine?
original.rationale: The Pin Index Safety System (PISS) uses a unique pin-hole configuration on the cylinder valve and yoke for each gas, physically preventing attachment of the wrong cylinder to the wrong yoke. DISS is used for pipeline connections (threaded, non-interchangeable connectors).

original.q: The fail-safe system on the anesthesia machine activates when oxygen pressure drops below ~25–30 psi. What does it do?
options: Activates an audible alarm only and continues delivering all gases
Shuts off all gas flow including oxygen
Reduces or shuts off flow of all non-oxygen gases to prevent a hypoxic mixture
Switches automatically to the backup E-cylinder oxygen supply
original.rationale: The fail-safe monitors O2 supply pressure and, when it drops below threshold, reduces or eliminates flow of N2O and air. It does NOT shut off oxygen itself, and it does NOT guarantee adequate O2 concentration — it only responds to supply pressure, not actual O2 concentration delivered to the patient.

original.q: During hospital construction, a pipeline crossover error results in nitrogen being delivered through the oxygen pipeline. The fail-safe system will:
options: Immediately alarm and shut down all gas flow
Fail to prevent delivery of a hypoxic gas mixture — it monitors pressure only
Detect the nitrogen and automatically switch to E-cylinder oxygen
Activate the oxygen ratio controller to compensate
original.rationale: The fail-safe system only responds to oxygen PRESSURE, not oxygen CONCENTRATION. If nitrogen is delivered through the O2 pipeline at 50–55 psi, the fail-safe sees adequate pressure and does not activate. This is a critical safety limitation — pipeline crossover errors are rare but catastrophic.

original.q: An E-cylinder of oxygen reads 1,500 psi. At a flow rate of 5 L/min, approximately how long will it last?
original.rationale: Use the formula: Duration (min) = [Pressure (psi) × 0.3] ÷ Flow rate (L/min). Therefore: (1,500 × 0.3) ÷ 5 = 450 ÷ 5 = 90 minutes. This formula applies only to oxygen (compressed gas); it cannot be used for N2O.

original.q: Which color coding correctly identifies medical oxygen pipeline and cylinder supply in the United States?
original.rationale: In the United States, oxygen is color-coded GREEN for both pipeline and cylinder supplies. Nitrous oxide is BLUE, medical air is YELLOW, and carbon dioxide is GRAY. Note: International color coding differs (e.g., oxygen is WHITE in most of Europe).

original.q: On North American anesthesia machines, which flowmeter is always positioned on the RIGHT (downstream, closest to the common gas outlet) and why?
options: Nitrous oxide — it must be last to blend with oxygen
Air — it is the most commonly used carrier gas
Oxygen — so that a manifold leak preferentially contaminates with O2, not a hypoxic gas
The position is not standardized and varies by manufacturer
original.rationale: Oxygen is always on the RIGHT (downstream position) on North American machines. If there is a crack or internal leak in the flowmeter manifold, the downstream gas (O2) will preferentially enter the fresh gas stream rather than the upstream hypoxic gas (N2O or air). This is a critical patient safety design feature.

original.q: The first-stage pressure regulator on the anesthesia machine reduces E-cylinder oxygen pressure from ~2,200 psi to approximately:
original.rationale: The first-stage (high-pressure) regulator at the cylinder yoke reduces E-cylinder pressure from ~2,200 psi down to ~45 psi — approximately matching pipeline pressure. This allows seamless switching between pipeline and cylinder supply. The second-stage regulator further reduces pressure to ~14–16 psi for the flowmeters.

original.q: A patient experiences laryngospasm during emergence. You activate the oxygen flush valve. Which statement is TRUE regarding this action?
options: It delivers 100% O2 at 2–5 L/min through the vaporizer
It delivers 100% O2 at 35–75 L/min, bypassing the vaporizer and flowmeters
It activates only if the pipeline O2 pressure is above 55 psi
It should not be used during spontaneous ventilation because it delivers room air
original.rationale: The O2 flush valve delivers 100% oxygen at 35–75 L/min directly from the pipeline, completely bypassing the flowmeters, vaporizer, and second-stage regulator. It should be used cautiously during IPPV (can cause barotrauma) and during spontaneous ventilation (the high flow can prevent exhalation and cause auto-PEEP). It dilutes anesthetic concentration in the circuit.

original.q: Which volatile anesthetic has the HIGHEST SVP (saturated vapor pressure) at room temperature and therefore requires the most precise agent-specific vaporizer control?
original.rationale: Desflurane has an SVP of ~669 mmHg — near atmospheric pressure — meaning it would vaporize explosively at room temperature if placed in a standard vaporizer. It requires a specialized, pressurized, heated vaporizer (e.g., Tec 6) that maintains the agent at 39°C. Its boiling point is only 22.8°C, close to room temperature.

original.q: During the anesthesia machine pre-use check, you perform a low-pressure system leak test. What does this test specifically assess?
options: The integrity of the high-pressure cylinder connections
Leaks between the flowmeters, vaporizer, and common gas outlet
The function of the fail-safe valve
original.rationale: The low-pressure leak test assesses the integrity of the low-pressure section — from the flowmeters through the vaporizer to the common gas outlet. This is the most important leak test because a leak here dilutes the fresh gas mixture without triggering any alarm.

original.q: In correct gas flow sequence through the anesthesia machine, where does the vaporizer sit relative to the flowmeters and the common gas outlet?
options: Between the fail-safe valve and the flowmeters
Downstream of the flowmeters, upstream of the common gas outlet
Parallel to the flowmeters with a mixing valve
original.rationale: The correct sequence is: Gas source → Pressure regulators → Fail-safe → Flowmeters → Vaporizer → Common gas outlet → Breathing circuit. The vaporizer sits downstream of the flowmeters and upstream of the fresh gas outlet. This ensures measured carrier gas flow picks up vapor before reaching the patient circuit.

original.q: The minimum oxygen ratio controller (e.g., Link-25) on the anesthesia machine is designed to:
options: Alarm when O2 flows exceed 8 L/min
Prevent setting a fresh gas mixture with less than 25% oxygen
Automatically increase oxygen flow when SpO2 drops below 94%
Disable the nitrous oxide flowmeter when E-cylinder O2 pressure is low
original.rationale: The minimum O2 ratio controller (Link-25 or Ratio-Master) mechanically or electronically links the N2O and O2 flow controls to ensure the delivered mixture contains at least 25% O2. If the clinician attempts to increase N2O beyond this ratio, O2 flow is automatically increased proportionally. This prevents accidental delivery of hypoxic mixtures.

original.q: Compound A forms when sevoflurane reacts with which CO2 absorbent under conditions of low flow and high temperature?
options: Soda lime containing NaOH and KOH
original.rationale: Compound A forms when sevoflurane reacts with strong bases, primarily KOH and NaOH found in traditional soda lime. Production increases with low fresh gas flow rates, high absorbent temperature, and desiccated absorbent. Amsorb Plus (calcium hydroxide only) does not contain NaOH/KOH and produces negligible Compound A.

original.q: A Mapleson D circuit is being used for a spontaneously breathing adult patient. To prevent rebreathing, the fresh gas flow should be:
options: Equal to the patient's tidal volume
original.rationale: The Mapleson D (and its modification, the Bain circuit) requires a fresh gas flow of approximately 2–3× the patient's minute ventilation to prevent CO2 rebreathing during spontaneous breathing. During controlled ventilation, it is more efficient, requiring only 70–100 mL/kg/min. The Mapleson A (Magill) is the most efficient for spontaneous breathing (FGF = 1× MV).

original.q: The active scavenging system in the OR removes waste anesthetic gases. If the interface reservoir bag is fully collapsed during exhalation, this indicates:
options: Normal function — the system is working correctly
Excessive positive pressure in the scavenging system — possible obstruction
Excessive negative pressure (suction too high) — risk of subatmospheric pressure reaching the patient circuit
The absorber is saturated and needs replacement
original.rationale: In an active scavenging system, the interface bag buffers waste gas flow. A fully collapsed bag indicates the vacuum (suction) is drawing more than the system is supplying — excessive negative pressure can be transmitted back to the breathing circuit, causing unintended PEEP removal or rebreathing. Conversely, a fully distended bag suggests inadequate suction or obstruction.

original.q: A patient with a suspected anterior larynx is being intubated. Which direct laryngoscopy blade and technique is MOST appropriate?
options: Macintosh blade — tip in vallecula, indirectly elevates epiglottis
Miller blade — tip passes posterior to the epiglottis and directly lifts it
McCoy blade — hinged tip activated to flex epiglottis
Either B or C — both directly elevate the epiglottis
original.rationale: Both the Miller (straight blade, tip posterior to epiglottis, direct lift) and McCoy (hinged Macintosh-style blade that flexes to lift epiglottis) directly elevate the epiglottis. These are preferred for anterior larynges, pediatric patients, and when Macintosh fails. The McCoy's hinged tip can improve Cormack-Lehane grade by 1–2 grades.

original.q: A Cormack-Lehane Grade III view on direct laryngoscopy reveals:
options: Only the posterior portion of the arytenoids visible
Only the epiglottis visible — glottis not seen
No laryngeal structures visible — only soft palate
original.rationale: The Cormack-Lehane grading system: Grade I = full glottis visible; Grade II = only posterior commissure/arytenoids visible; Grade III = only epiglottis visible, glottis not seen; Grade IV = epiglottis not visible, only soft palate. Grades III–IV are associated with difficult intubation and require alternative techniques.

original.q: Which video laryngoscope is specifically designed for use WITHOUT a stylet due to its low angle of curvature, making it most suitable for routine intubations?
options: GlideScope (standard blade) — high curvature requires stylet
C-MAC (standard blade) — low curvature, direct-style view, stylet optional
Airtraq — optical device, no stylet needed
original.rationale: The C-MAC with a standard Mac-style blade provides an indirect video view while maintaining the low curvature of a standard Macintosh blade. A stylet is often not required, making it suitable for both routine and difficult airway management. The GlideScope standard blade has a 60° curvature requiring a specifically shaped stylet.

original.q: During awake fiberoptic intubation (AFOI), topical anesthesia of the airway is performed. Which nerve blocks provide anesthesia to the SUPRAGLOTTIC structures (tongue base, epiglottis, vallecula)?
original.rationale: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory innervation to the posterior tongue, vallecula, and epiglottis (supraglottic structures). Superior laryngeal nerve (internal branch) blocks anesthetize the larynx down to the vocal cords. Transtracheal injection anesthetizes the subglottic trachea. Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensory innervation below the cords.

original.q: When performing fiberoptic-guided intubation through an LMA in a 'cannot intubate' scenario, the MINIMUM LMA size needed to pass a standard 8.0 mm ETT is approximately:
options: Any size LMA can accommodate an 8.0 ETT
original.rationale: A size 5 LMA Classic (or equivalent) is the minimum size that can accommodate a standard 8.0 mm ETT through the LMA barrel during fiberoptic-guided intubation. Size 3 and 4 LMAs have internal diameters that limit passage to size 6.0 and 6.5 ETTs, respectively.

original.q: You are intubating an 8-year-old child. Using the age-based formula, what is the appropriate UNCUFFED ETT size?
original.rationale: The standard formula for uncuffed ETT size in children is (Age in years ÷ 4) + 4. For an 8-year-old: (8 ÷ 4) + 4 = 2 + 4 = 6.0 mm. Always have the next size up (6.5) and down (5.5) available. For cuffed ETTs, the formula is (Age ÷ 4) + 3.5, giving 5.5 mm for an 8-year-old.

original.q: The recommended ETT cuff pressure range to minimize tracheal mucosal ischemia while maintaining an adequate seal is:
original.rationale: ETT cuff pressure should be maintained between 20–30 cmH2O. Below 20 cmH2O, the cuff may not provide an adequate seal, risking aspiration and air leak. Above 30 cmH2O, lateral tracheal wall pressure may exceed mucosal capillary perfusion pressure (~25–35 mmHg), leading to mucosal ischemia, necrosis, and potential tracheal stenosis.

original.q: A thoracic surgery patient requires one-lung ventilation. A left-sided double-lumen tube (DLT) is placed. Which bronchus will the bronchial lumen intubate?
options: Right mainstem bronchus — the larger bronchus
Left mainstem bronchus — the bronchial lumen is passed into the left bronchus
Either bronchus — DLT selection is based on patient size only
The trachea — one lumen sits in the trachea and one in the right main bronchus
original.rationale: A left-sided DLT has a curved bronchial tip designed to pass into the LEFT mainstem bronchus. The tracheal lumen opens into the trachea above the carina, ventilating the right lung. A right-sided DLT is reserved for specific indications (left-sided pneumonectomy, left bronchial anomaly) because the right upper lobe bronchus origin is close to the carina.

original.q: Which specialized ETT is MOST appropriate for a patient requiring continuous subglottic suctioning to reduce the risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)?
options: Evac/subglottic suction ETT (e.g., Mallinckrodt Hi-Lo Evac)
original.rationale: Subglottic suction ETTs (e.g., Hi-Lo Evac, SealGuard Evac) have an additional dorsal lumen that exits just above the cuff, allowing continuous or intermittent aspiration of secretions that pool above the cuff. This significantly reduces VAP risk in mechanically ventilated patients.

original.q: You are preparing for airway laser surgery of the larynx. Standard PVC ETTs are contraindicated. What is the PRIMARY reason?
options: PVC tubes are too rigid and obstruct the surgical field
PVC is highly flammable and can ignite in the oxygen-enriched environment with laser energy
PVC tubes do not provide an adequate cuff seal at high inflation pressures
The laser cannot be used near standard cuffs filled with air
original.rationale: PVC (polyvinyl chloride) ETTs are combustible and can ignite when struck by laser energy in an oxygen- or nitrous oxide-enriched environment, causing an airway fire. Laser-safe ETTs are constructed from stainless steel, silicone-coated metal, or have a foil-wrapped outer layer. The cuff should be filled with saline rather than air.

original.q: A 2nd-generation supraglottic airway device differs from a 1st-generation device primarily by:
options: Having a smaller cuff volume and lower oropharyngeal leak pressure
Incorporating a gastric drainage channel and higher oropharyngeal leak pressures (>25 cmH2O)
Being designed exclusively for pediatric patients
original.rationale: 2nd-generation SGAs (e.g., ProSeal LMA, Supreme LMA, i-gel) incorporate a gastric access/drainage channel that allows passage of a gastric tube to decompress the stomach, reducing aspiration risk. They also achieve higher oropharyngeal leak pressures (typically >25–27 cmH2O), making them more suitable for positive-pressure ventilation.

original.q: The i-gel supraglottic airway is unique among SGAs because:
options: It has the largest cuff volume of any commercially available SGA
It uses a non-inflatable, gel-like thermoplastic elastomer cuff that molds to the laryngeal anatomy
It can only be used in patients weighing over 70 kg
It requires a rigid introducer for insertion in all cases
original.rationale: The i-gel (Intersurgical) uses a non-inflatable cuff made of a soft, gel-like thermoplastic elastomer (SEBS). Body heat causes the cuff to soften and conform to the perilaryngeal anatomy, creating a seal without inflation. It also incorporates a gastric drainage channel (2nd-generation), epiglottic rest, and bite block.

original.q: You plan to use an LMA-Fastrach (intubating LMA) for a patient with a predicted difficult airway. The maximum ETT size that can be passed through the standard Fastrach is:
original.rationale: The LMA-Fastrach (ILMA) has a rigid curved shaft with a 13 mm internal diameter channel designed to accommodate ETTs up to 8.0 mm (cuffed). It is used with a specific silicone wire-reinforced ETT (LMA Fastrach ETT) that is designed to navigate the curve of the Fastrach.

original.q: When inserting a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA), the correct size in adults is estimated by measuring from the:
options: Corner of the mouth to the ear tragus
Tip of the nose to the ear tragus
Nasal tip to the angle of the mandible
original.rationale: NPA size is estimated by measuring from the tip of the nose to the tragus of the ear. This approximates the distance from the naris to the nasopharynx. Oral airways (OPAs) are sized from the corner of the mouth to the ear tragus. Using the wrong landmark is a common exam question.

original.q: A patient presents in extremis after failed oral and nasal intubation attempts. The preferred emergency front-of-neck access (eFONA) technique in most CICO scenarios is:
options: Percutaneous needle cricothyrotomy with jet ventilation
Surgical scalpel-bougie-tube technique through the cricothyroid membrane
Retrograde wire intubation via the cricothyroid membrane
original.rationale: Current DAS (Difficult Airway Society) and most major guidelines recommend the scalpel-bougie-tube (surgical) technique as the preferred eFONA in CICO emergencies. A horizontal stab incision is made through the cricothyroid membrane, a bougie is inserted, and a size 6.0 cuffed ETT is railroaded over the bougie. It is reliable, fast, and does not require specialized kits.

original.q: High-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO/THRIVE) during apneic oxygenation can extend the safe apnea time during intubation. The mechanism by which HFNO maintains oxygenation during apnea is primarily:
options: Active ventilation via the Venturi effect in the nasopharynx
Apneic oxygenation — O2 diffuses down an oxygen concentration gradient into the alveoli without respiratory effort
Generation of positive pressure that splints the alveoli open
Absorption of alveolar CO2 by the high oxygen flow
original.rationale: Apneic oxygenation works because O2 consumption continues (~250 mL/min) during apnea, creating a concentration gradient that draws O2 from the upper airway into the alveoli by mass flow, even without respiratory effort. HFNO delivers 40–70 L/min of warmed, humidified O2 to continuously replenish the nasopharyngeal oxygen reservoir.

original.q: In Pressure-Controlled Ventilation (PCV), which parameter is set directly by the clinician?
options: Respiratory rate and I:E ratio only
original.rationale: In PCV, the clinician sets the peak inspiratory pressure (driving pressure), respiratory rate, and I:E ratio. Tidal volume is the dependent variable — it varies based on lung compliance and airway resistance. PCV is useful when limiting peak pressures is a priority (e.g., ARDS, lung-protective ventilation). In contrast, in VCV, tidal volume is set and peak pressure varies.

original.q: A patient under general anesthesia has a plateau pressure of 38 cmH2O and a peak airway pressure of 42 cmH2O. What does the elevated plateau pressure (>30 cmH2O) most likely indicate?
options: Decreased lung/chest wall compliance (atelectasis, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema)
original.rationale: Plateau pressure reflects static lung/chest wall compliance — it is measured at end-inspiration with flow stopped. Elevated plateau pressure (>30 cmH2O) indicates decreased compliance: pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, endobronchial intubation, abdominal distension. Elevated PEAK pressure with NORMAL plateau pressure indicates increased airway resistance. This distinction is critical on the NBCRNA exam.

original.q: According to ASA basic monitoring standards, which monitor is required during EVERY anesthetic (including MAC/monitored anesthesia care)?
original.rationale: ASA basic monitoring standards require continuous pulse oximetry (SpO2), continuous capnography (ETCO2) when intubated, ECG, blood pressure at least every 5 minutes, temperature when changes are anticipated, and an inspired O2 analyzer. BIS, NMB monitoring, and arterial lines are advanced monitors — not ASA standard requirements.

original.q: A Line Isolation Monitor (LIM) in the OR alarms. This indicates:
options: A patient has suffered a macroshock electrical injury
The first fault condition has occurred — the isolated power system has a pathway to ground
An electrical device has shorted and must be removed immediately
The OR power supply has failed and the backup generator is activated
original.rationale: The OR uses an isolated power system (no direct connection to earth ground) to reduce electrocution risk. A LIM alarms when it signals the FIRST fault — a single pathway to ground has been created. The patient is NOT in immediate danger from the first fault alone. The dangerous situation is the SECOND fault — which would complete a circuit through the patient. The faulty device should be identified and removed.

original.q: The minimum amount of current required to cause ventricular fibrillation when applied DIRECTLY to the myocardium (microshock) is approximately:
original.rationale: Microshock (current directly to myocardium via cardiac catheter, pacing wires, or intracardiac catheters) can cause ventricular fibrillation with as little as 100 mcA (microamperes = 0.1 mA). Macroshock (current through intact skin) requires approximately 100 mA to fibrillate. This 1,000-fold difference is why patients with intracardiac catheters require the isolated power system and extra electrical precautions.

original.q: Processed EEG monitoring (e.g., BIS) in the OR is primarily used to:
options: Assess depth of hypnosis and reduce awareness under general anesthesia
Monitor cerebral oxygenation during carotid endarterectomy
original.rationale: Bispectral Index (BIS) and similar processed EEG monitors provide a dimensionless score (0–100). BIS 40–60 correlates with adequate hypnotic depth for general anesthesia; BIS >60 may indicate light anesthesia and increased awareness risk; BIS <40 indicates deep suppression. Cerebral oximetry (rSO2 via NIRS) monitors cerebral oxygenation in carotid surgery.

original.q: A patient develops a postdural puncture headache (PDPH) 24 hours after spinal anesthesia. Which needle type is associated with the LOWEST incidence of PDPH?
original.rationale: Pencil-point needles (Whitacre, Sprotte) spread dural fibers apart rather than cutting them, allowing the dura to reseal more effectively after withdrawal. They have significantly lower PDPH rates than cutting-tip (Quincke) needles of the same gauge. Smaller gauge also reduces PDPH risk. The Tuohy (used for epidural) has the highest PDPH risk if it inadvertently punctures the dura.

original.q: For ultrasound-guided nerve blocks of deep structures (e.g., sciatic nerve, lumbar plexus), which ultrasound probe is preferred?
options: High-frequency linear probe (10–15 MHz) — better resolution for deep structures
Low-frequency curvilinear probe (2–5 MHz) — greater penetration depth
Phased array probe (1–5 MHz) — designed for cardiac imaging
Hockey-stick linear probe (13–6 MHz) — designed specifically for nerve blocks
original.rationale: Low-frequency curvilinear (convex) probes (2–5 MHz) provide greater tissue penetration (up to 10–15 cm), making them suitable for deep structures like the sciatic nerve, lumbar plexus, and psoas compartment. High-frequency linear probes (6–15 MHz) provide excellent resolution for superficial structures but have limited penetration (3–4 cm).

original.q: During a nerve stimulator-guided peripheral nerve block, what is the optimal endpoint (motor response) indicating correct needle tip placement for local anesthetic injection?
options: A strong motor twitch at 1.5–2.0 mA
A visible motor twitch at 0.2–0.5 mA with loss of twitch at 0.1 mA
No motor response at any current level
original.rationale: The optimal endpoint is eliciting the appropriate motor response (twitch) at a current of 0.2–0.5 mA. If a twitch is obtained at <0.2 mA (especially if injection resistance is high), the needle may be intraneural — the needle should be withdrawn slightly before injecting. Loss of twitch at ≥0.5 mA suggests the needle is too far from the nerve.

original.q: A patient is hemorrhaging and requires the fastest possible fluid resuscitation. Which catheter size delivers the greatest flow rate?
original.rationale: Per Poiseuille's law, flow is proportional to the radius to the 4th power. An 8.5 Fr introducer sheath (cordis) has an internal lumen substantially larger than even a 14G peripheral IV and can deliver fluid at rates exceeding 500 mL/min with pressure. Among peripheral IVs: 14G (>250 mL/min) > 16G (~180 mL/min) > 18G (~90 mL/min).

original.q: An arterial line is placed in the radial artery for continuous blood pressure monitoring. Before placing a radial arterial line, the modified Allen's test is performed to assess:
options: Adequate collateral ulnar circulation to the hand
Presence of a normal radial pulse waveform
Patency of the palmar arches bilaterally
original.rationale: The modified Allen's test assesses whether the ulnar artery can provide adequate collateral perfusion to the hand if the radial artery is occluded by the arterial line or damaged during insertion. Return of color within 5–7 seconds after releasing ulnar pressure indicates adequate ulnar collateral flow. A negative Allen's test (>15 seconds or no return) suggests inadequate collateral circulation.

original.q: A TIVA infusion of propofol is running via a target-controlled infusion (TCI) pump. Which pharmacokinetic model is most commonly used for propofol TCI in adults?
options: Marsh model — uses weight-based compartment calculations
Schnider model — incorporates weight, height, age, and lean body mass
Shafer-Varvel model — designed specifically for pediatric propofol dosing
Minto model — developed for remifentanil TCI
original.rationale: The Schnider model (1998) incorporates patient covariates including total body weight, height, age, and derived lean body mass (LBM) to calculate propofol distribution and clearance. It targets plasma (Cp) or effect-site (Ce) concentration. The Marsh model (1991) uses only body weight. The Minto model is used for remifentanil TCI.

original.q: SITUATIONAL: After RSI and ETT placement for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, you note SpO2 declining and bilateral breath sounds are absent on the LEFT. ETCO2 waveform is present. The MOST likely cause and immediate action is:
options: Esophageal intubation — remove ETT and ventilate by mask
Right mainstem endobronchial intubation — withdraw the ETT 2–3 cm
Left-sided tension pneumothorax — needle decompression 2nd ICS MCL
Kinked ETT — replace with a new tube
original.rationale: ETCO2 confirms tracheal placement (eliminating esophageal intubation). Absent breath sounds on the LEFT with present ETCO2 and declining SpO2 after RSI strongly suggests right mainstem endobronchial intubation — the ETT has advanced too far into the right main bronchus, excluding the left lung. The right mainstem is shorter, straighter, and larger — the most common site of endobronchial intubation. Withdraw the ETT 2–3 cm while auscultating.

original.q: SITUATIONAL: Mid-case, the O2 supply pipeline fails. You switch to E-cylinder oxygen. The E-cylinder reads 900 psi. Your patient is on 3 L/min O2. Approximately how long before the E-cylinder runs out?
original.rationale: Using the E-cylinder duration formula: Duration (min) = [Pressure (psi) × 0.3] ÷ Flow rate (L/min). Duration = (900 × 0.3) ÷ 3 = 270 ÷ 3 = 90 minutes. This gives approximately 90 minutes — enough time to complete most cases or arrange for a new cylinder/pipeline restoration.

original.q: SITUATIONAL: A 52-year-old male presents for elective rhinoplasty with Mallampati III, limited mouth opening (2 cm), short thyromental distance, and a beard. He has no known difficult airway history. The MOST appropriate plan is:
options: Standard RSI with direct laryngoscopy — Mallampati III alone is rarely problematic
Awake fiberoptic intubation with topical airway anesthesia and dexmedetomidine sedation
Video laryngoscopy with a hyperangulated blade after standard induction, with a surgical airway kit immediately available
LMA placement — rhinoplasty does not require intubation
original.rationale: Multiple predictors of difficult airway are present: Mallampati III, limited mouth opening (2 cm — normal is ≥3.5 cm), short thyromental distance, and beard. The combination of 2–3 independent difficult airway predictors with difficult bag-mask ventilation indicators warrants an awake technique. AFOI with topical anesthesia and light dexmedetomidine sedation is the gold-standard for anticipated difficult airway management.

original.q: SITUATIONAL: During a 4-hour open abdominal case, the CO2 absorbent granules turn PURPLE/VIOLET. The ETCO2 is rising (55 mmHg) despite unchanged ventilator settings. What is the correct interpretation and action?
options: Normal color change — no action needed, replace absorbent at end of case
Absorbent is exhausted — replace the CO2 absorbent immediately to prevent hypercapnia and rebreathing
Sevoflurane has reacted with the absorbent — stop sevoflurane, switch to TIVA
The color change indicates moisture loss — increase fresh gas flow to compensate
original.rationale: CO2 absorbents contain a pH-sensitive color indicator. Fresh absorbent is white/off-white; when exhausted, the indicator turns VIOLET/PURPLE (soda lime). Rising ETCO2 with unchanged ventilator settings = CO2 rebreathing from exhausted absorbent. Replace immediately. Note: some absorbents can paradoxically return to white when CO2 is no longer being absorbed ("regeneration") — the granules can appear white but be functionally exhausted; always check ETCO2.

original.q: A 68-year-old with ESRD receives rocuronium 0.6 mg/kg. After 4 hours, which reversal is MOST appropriate?
options: Neostigmine 0.05 mg/kg with glycopyrrolate — standard reversal at 4 hours
Sugammadex 2 mg/kg — at T2 recovery, regardless of renal status
Sugammadex 4 mg/kg — renal failure prolongs rocuronium but sugammadex is still preferred
Neostigmine alone — glycopyrrolate should be avoided in renal failure
original.rationale: Sugammadex 4 mg/kg is preferred in ESRD. Renal failure prolongs rocuronium; sugammadex provides complete, quantifiable reversal superior to neostigmine. Use 4 mg/kg (not 2 mg/kg) for more complete reversal at shallow block in ESRD, and monitor for re-curarization.

original.q: Bupivacaine 0.5% epidural causes sudden cardiovascular collapse with wide-complex dysrhythmia. The MOST critical immediate intervention?
original.rationale: LAST from bupivacaine — the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic. Intralipid 20% 1.5 mL/kg bolus then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion creates a "lipid sink" sequestering bupivacaine. Amiodarone is NOT recommended in LAST — it inhibits Na+ channels and may worsen toxicity.

original.q: During one-lung ventilation (left lateral decubitus), a patient develops hypoxemia. Which mechanism BEST explains the initial compensatory response?
options: Increased cardiac output to the dependent lung
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) in the non-dependent lung
Increased tidal volume to the dependent lung
Reflex bronchodilation in the non-dependent lung
original.rationale: HPV is the primary compensatory mechanism. When the non-dependent lung is deflated (alveolar hypoxia), HPV causes vasoconstriction, diverting blood to the ventilated lung. Volatile agents blunt HPV and worsen hypoxemia.

original.q: Sevoflurane 2% with desiccated CO2 absorbent (soda lime). Which MOST dangerous compound is produced?
original.rationale: Desiccated soda lime (especially with NaOH/KOH) reacts with volatiles to produce carbon monoxide — most immediately life-threatening. Desflurane and isoflurane produce the most CO with desiccated soda lime; sevoflurane produces compound A at low (non-desiccated) flows.

original.q: A patient with PFO undergoes posterior fossa craniotomy (sitting). ETCO2 drops to 22 mmHg and mill-wheel murmur is heard. The MOST dangerous complication specific to the PFO?
options: Paradoxical air embolism causing stroke or coronary air embolism
Systemic air embolism from arterial line
original.rationale: VAE + PFO = paradoxical embolism risk. Air crossing from right atrium to left atrium (via PFO) can cause arterial air embolism — stroke, coronary air embolism, or other end-organ ischemia. This occurs when right atrial pressure exceeds left atrial pressure.
